part2.modelAnswer: Well, I'd like to talk about my uncle who really helped me during a difficult period in my life. He's my father's younger brother, and he's quite a successful businessman living in the city. A few years ago, I was going through a really challenging time because I'd just failed my university entrance exam, and I was feeling quite down and unmotivated about everything. I didn't know what my next steps should be, and I was really doubting my abilities. So, my uncle came to visit us, and instead of just sympathizing with me, he sat down and had a long conversation with me about my goals and what I actually wanted to achieve. He shared his own experiences of failure, which was quite eye-opening, and he encouraged me to see it as a learning opportunity rather than a setback. He even offered to help me find a good tutor and supported me financially during my preparation for the next attempt. Thanks to his guidance and encouragement, I eventually passed the exam and got into a university. To be honest, I felt immensely grateful for his support, not just because of the practical help, but because he believed in me when I didn't believe in myself. It really strengthened our relationship, and I learned that sometimes we all need someone to lift us up and remind us of our potential.

part2.modelAnswer: I'm going to tell you about Kyoto, which I visited last year with my family. It's an ancient city in Japan that was once the imperial capital. We spent about a week there during the spring season, and it was absolutely fantastic. During our stay, we visited numerous temples and shrines, and what really struck me was the sheer beauty and tranquility of these places. We spent hours wandering through the famous Fushimi Inari shrine with its thousands of red torii gates, and we also visited some traditional gardens that were simply breathtaking. One of my favourite activities was actually staying in a traditional ryokan, which is a Japanese inn, and experiencing the culture firsthand. We had authentic Japanese meals and even got to wear traditional kimonos. What I found particularly interesting about Kyoto was the way it seamlessly blends ancient tradition with modern life. Despite being a bustling city, it has managed to preserve its cultural heritage beautifully. The architectural style, the gardens, the tea ceremonies we witnessed – all of it gave me a deep appreciation for Japanese aesthetics and philosophy. I think what really captivated me was the sense of peace and mindfulness that the entire place seemed to emanate. It was genuinely one of the most enriching travel experiences I've had.

My grandfather had used this pen for decades, and he decided to pass it on to me when I was completing my university studies. He told me that it brought him luck throughout his career and that he hoped it would do the same for me. I don't use it for everyday writing because I want to preserve it, but I do use it occasionally for important documents or when I'm writing something particularly meaningful. To be perfectly honest, what makes this object so special to me is not just its material value, but the emotional connection it represents. Every time I hold it, I feel connected to my grandfather's wisdom and his belief in my future. He was a journalist, very well-respected, and I think he wanted me to carry on his legacy of expressing myself through writing. After his death, this pen became even more precious because it's one of the few tangible things I have that belonged to him. It reminds me of his values – integrity, precision, and the power of words. I keep it in a special drawer, and sometimes I take it out just to remember him and reflect on the lessons he taught me.

part2.modelAnswer: Right, so I'd like to talk about helping my neighbour, Mrs. Chen, about two years ago. She's an elderly woman in her seventies who lives alone, and her son is usually abroad for work. One winter, she had a bad fall in her house and broke her wrist quite severely. At that time, I was a university student living back with my parents, so I had some flexibility with my schedule. When I heard about her accident, I immediately went to check on her and found that she was in considerable pain and couldn't do basic tasks like cooking or cleaning. So, I made the decision to help her out for about two weeks until she recovered enough to manage on her own. During those two weeks, I'd visit her place every day, sometimes twice a day. I'd prepare meals for her, help her with housework, accompany her to medical appointments, and just keep her company so she wouldn't feel lonely. It wasn't particularly difficult work, but it required patience and genuine care. What I felt during this whole experience was a strong sense of fulfilment and purpose. To be honest, I realized that helping someone in genuine need is deeply rewarding, not in a material sense, but emotionally. It made me appreciate my own good health and my family's support. Mrs. Chen was incredibly grateful, and we developed a much closer bond. This experience definitely shaped my perspective on community responsibility and the importance of looking out for vulnerable people around us.

It probably took me around six months of consistent practice before I felt reasonably confident with manual mode on my camera. However, I'm still learning even now, as photography is quite a deep field with always something new to discover. As for why I decided to pursue this skill, well, it started as a way to express my creativity in a different way. I've always enjoyed visual arts, but photography felt more accessible to me than painting or drawing. Over time, it became a therapeutic hobby as well – whenever I'm stressed or overwhelmed with work, I go out with my camera and just explore my surroundings. It's really helped me develop a different perspective on the world, noticing details I might have otherwise missed. Now I occasionally do some freelance work for friends and small events, which is quite rewarding. I think learning this skill has genuinely enriched my life in unexpected ways.

part2.modelAnswer: I'd like to talk about a book called 'Educated' by Tara Westover, which I read last year. It's a memoir about the author's journey from being raised in a survivalist family with no formal education to eventually attending Cambridge University. I actually picked it up quite by chance when a friend recommended it, and I couldn't put it down. The book chronicles her early life in Idaho where her father was a fundamentalist believer, and she was kept isolated from mainstream society. The narrative follows her decision to pursue education despite intense family opposition and the psychological challenges she faced in adapting to mainstream school and university life. What I found absolutely compelling about this book was the raw honesty with which Westover describes her transformation. Reading about her struggle with cognitive dissonance – between her family's beliefs and what she learned in school – was quite profound. She doesn't paint her parents as simple villains; rather, she presents a nuanced picture of family dynamics and ideology. What made me really enjoy this book was that it goes beyond just being a survival story. It's fundamentally about the power of education to transform lives and the courage it takes to challenge deeply ingrained beliefs. Her writing style is quite accessible yet philosophically rich, which I really appreciated. The book also made me reflect on my own privilege in receiving education without obstacles. Since reading it, I've been much more aware of educational inequalities globally. I'd definitely recommend it to anyone interested in personal narratives of transformation and overcoming adversity.

part2.modelAnswer: I recently watched a film called 'Parasite', which is a South Korean film directed by Bong Joon-ho. I saw it at the cinema about a month ago with some friends from university. The film is a brilliant social thriller that tells the story of a poor family that schemes their way into employment with a wealthy family. The narrative is quite complex – the Kim family gradually infiltrates the Park family's household by pretending to be unrelated, highly qualified workers, and the film explores the class tensions and moral ambiguities that arise from this deception. What I found particularly brilliant about this film was the way it seamlessly blends multiple genres – it's partly a black comedy, partly a thriller, and partly a profound social commentary on inequality. The director uses visual storytelling incredibly effectively. For instance, the spatial relationships between the two families' homes are constantly emphasized, and this visual metaphor of class hierarchy is woven throughout the entire film. The cinematography is absolutely stunning as well. I really enjoyed watching it because it made me think critically about class structures and economic inequality in a way that felt both entertaining and thought-provoking. Unlike some films that preach political messages, 'Parasite' lets the audience draw their own conclusions. The performances from all the actors were phenomenal too – there was a genuine sense of chemistry and tension between the characters. To be honest, it's one of those films that stays with you after you've finished watching it, and I've already discussed it extensively with my friends because there's so much to unpack and analyze.

part2.modelAnswer: One of the most important events in my life was when I graduated from secondary school and passed my university entrance examination. This happened about four years ago, and it was a turning point for me in many ways. This event involved not just myself, but my entire family, particularly my parents and teachers who had supported me throughout my schooling. The actual day of the exam results was quite emotional – when I found out that I'd passed and got into my first-choice university, I felt an overwhelming sense of relief and achievement. To provide some context, I come from a family where I was the first person in my family to go to university. My parents had worked incredibly hard to provide me with good education, and there were certainly moments during my final year when I doubted whether I could succeed. This achievement was important to me for several reasons. Firstly, it represented the culmination of years of hard work and dedication. Secondly, it opened up opportunities that wouldn't have been available otherwise – university education expanded my horizons and allowed me to pursue my genuine interests. Thirdly, and perhaps most significantly, it validated my parents' investment in my education and their sacrifices. Beyond the personal achievement, this event was a turning point in my life because it represented a transition to adulthood and independence. Moving to university meant leaving home and learning to navigate life on my own. The experience also instilled in me a deeper sense of responsibility and purpose. Since that event, I've become much more aware of how privileged I am and how important it is to make the most of these opportunities. It fundamentally shaped my current goals and aspirations.

part2.modelAnswer: I'd like to describe the tradition of Tet, which is the Vietnamese Lunar New Year celebration that's central to my family's cultural identity. Tet is celebrated once a year, typically in late January or February depending on the lunar calendar, and the celebration usually lasts for about a week, though the most significant days are the first three days of the new lunar year. The celebration involves multiple rituals and activities. Traditionally, families prepare special foods – we make a particular sticky rice cake called bánh chưng. We also clean our houses thoroughly to symbolize getting rid of bad luck and starting fresh. On the eve of Tet, we arrange offerings for our ancestors and pay respects. We gather for special meals, and it's customary to visit relatives and friends. Everyone wears new clothes, and children receive small gifts of money in red envelopes. Who participates really varies – immediate family members always participate actively, but often extended family members come together as well. For me, this tradition is deeply meaningful for several reasons. Firstly, it's a time when the entire extended family makes a conscious effort to be together, which in our modern dispersed society is increasingly rare. Secondly, it connects me to my cultural heritage and my ancestors. When I'm preparing bánh chưng following my grandmother's recipe or paying respects to ancestors, I feel connected to generations before me. Thirdly, the tradition embodies important values – renewal, gratitude, family loyalty, and hope for the future. Even though I now live away from Vietnam for studies, observing Tet, even in a modified way, reminds me of who I am and where I come from. It's a tradition that grounds me culturally and emotionally.

We hired a small room above a family-run restaurant near the school, and there must have been about twenty of us squeezed around two long tables. Our form teacher came along as well, which was a nice surprise, because she wasn't usually very sociable outside lessons. The food itself was fairly simple: a big pot of soup to share, grilled fish, rice and lots of vegetable dishes, followed by a cake one of the parents had baked. I remember it mainly because of the atmosphere rather than the food. Everyone knew we were about to go our separate ways, so there was a mixture of excitement and sadness in the room. At one point the teacher stood up and gave a short speech about each of us, and quite a few people ended up in tears. Looking back, it was probably the last time the whole class was together, so it has stayed with me.
part2.band6: I will talk about a dinner with my classmates at the end of high school. We went to a small restaurant near our school, it was a family restaurant and we were maybe twenty people. Our teacher also come with us, and it was surprise because normally she is not very friendly outside class. We ate soup, fish, rice and many vegetables, and one mother made a cake for us. The food was delicious but I remember this meal because of the feeling. Everybody was happy and also sad because after that we go to different universities. Our teacher made a speech and she talked about every student, and many people cried. I think it was the last time all my class was together. So that is why I remember this dinner very well, it was a very special day for me.

notes.fc: Both answers cover the bullets in order. Band 6 states 'happy and also sad' plainly; band 7 develops the feeling ('a mixture of excitement and sadness', 'go our separate ways') and keeps a clear thread to the final reason.
notes.lr: Band 7 shows collocation and idiom control: 'squeezed around', 'family-run', 'ended up in tears', 'stayed with me'. Band 6 uses mostly high-frequency words ('nice', 'special', 'very').
notes.gra: Band 6: 'Our teacher also come', 'it was surprise', 'after that we go'. Band 7 uses modal deduction ('there must have been'), passive-like structures and non-defining relative clauses without error.

part2.cue: Describe a goal you hope to achieve in the next few years.

and explain how you will feel if you achieve it

part2.modelAnswer: One goal I'm working towards at the moment is completing a half-marathon within the next two years. I've never thought of myself as a sporty person, but during a long period of working from home I realised I was spending almost the whole day sitting down, and my energy levels had dropped noticeably. A colleague who runs regularly suggested I try a beginner's plan, and I was surprised how quickly I began to enjoy it. At the moment I'm running three times a week, gradually increasing the distance, and I've joined a local running group that meets on Sunday mornings, which keeps me motivated when the weather is miserable. I've also started paying more attention to what I eat and how much I sleep, because I've learned that recovery matters as much as the training itself. If I manage to cross the finish line, I think I'll feel enormously proud, partly because it's something I would have considered impossible a few years ago. It would also prove to me that steady, small steps can lead to quite big changes.
part2.band6: My goal is to run a half-marathon in the next two years. Before I was not a sporty person, but when I work from home I sit all day and I feel very tired. My colleague is a runner and she said I should try running, and I start to like it quickly. Now I run three times every week and every time I run a bit more far. Also I joined a running club and we run on Sunday morning, this is good for motivation especially when the weather is bad. I also try to eat healthy and sleep more. If I finish the half-marathon I will be very proud of myself, because few years ago I think it is impossible for me. So it is a big goal for me and I hope I can do it.

notes.fc: Band 6 is fluent but relies on 'also' and 'so' for linking. Band 7 links cause and effect more precisely ('because I've learned that', 'partly because', 'which keeps me motivated').

notes.gra: Band 6: tense errors ('when I work from home I sit', 'I start to like', 'few years ago I think it is impossible'). Band 7 handles present perfect, past perfect and the third-conditional-style 'would have considered' accurately.

part2.cue: Describe a place in your town or city where people go to relax.
bullets: and explain why it is a good place to relax
part3: Why do people in cities find it harder to relax than people in the countryside?
Should governments spend money on public spaces such as parks and squares?
Do you think people today have less free time than in the past?
How do different age groups prefer to relax?

part2.modelAnswer: The place I'd like to describe is a riverside path that runs along the edge of the old part of my city. It stretches for about three kilometres, and on one side there's the river while on the other there are rows of trees and a few small cafés with outdoor seating. A few years ago the area was quite run-down, but the local council cleaned it up, added benches and lighting, and now it's one of the most popular spots in town. In the early morning you'll mostly see joggers and people walking their dogs, whereas in the evening it's full of families, couples strolling along and older people chatting on the benches. At weekends there are sometimes street musicians as well. I think it works so well as a place to relax because it gives you a feeling of open space in the middle of a crowded city. The sound of the water seems to block out the traffic noise, and since it's free and open to everyone, nobody feels they have to spend money to enjoy it.
part2.band6: I want to describe the river path in my city. It is in the old town and it is about three kilometres long. On one side is the river and on the other side there are trees and some cafés. Before it was dirty and not nice, but the government cleaned it and now there are many benches and lights, so it is very popular. In the morning many people do jogging and walk with their dogs, and in the evening there are many families and old people who sit and talk. Sometimes on weekend there are musicians playing music. I think it is good for relaxing because the city is very crowded and here you can feel more space. Also you can hear the river and not the traffic. And it is free, everybody can go there, so I like it very much.

notes.fc: Band 6 describes in short, separate statements. Band 7 contrasts times of day with 'whereas' and gives a two-part explanation, so the answer flows as one argument.

part2.modelAnswer: A time that springs to mind is when I was waiting for the results of a medical test a couple of years ago. I'd had some tests done after a routine check-up, and the doctor told me they'd need to look more closely at one of the results, which would take about ten days. Most of that waiting happened at home and at work, carrying on with ordinary life while knowing a phone call could come at any moment. To be honest, the first few days were the hardest. I kept searching for information online, which only made me more anxious, so in the end a friend persuaded me to stop reading and to keep busy instead. I went swimming every evening and threw myself into a project at work, which helped a lot. When the call finally came, it turned out to be nothing serious, and I felt an enormous wave of relief. What I took away from it was that worrying doesn't change the outcome, and that it's better to focus on the things you can actually control.

part2.modelAnswer: The advice I'd like to talk about came from my first manager, when I'd just started a part-time job in a bookshop during my studies. I was very keen to impress, so I said yes to every request and ended up working far more hours than I'd agreed to, while my coursework started to suffer. After a few weeks she took me aside and told me something I've never forgotten: 'If you agree to everything, your yes stops meaning anything.' She explained that people respect you more when you're honest about what you can realistically do. At first I felt a bit embarrassed, because I thought I'd been doing a good job, but I soon realised she was right. I started being clearer about my availability, and surprisingly nobody minded. The reason it's been so helpful is that it applies to almost every part of life, from group projects at university to arrangements with friends. Learning to say no politely has made me less stressed, and I think it's actually made me more reliable, because now I only promise what I can deliver.

part2.modelAnswer: I'd like to describe a conversation I had on an overnight train a few years ago. I was travelling to visit relatives, and the woman sitting opposite me turned out to be a retired engineer who had helped design several of the bridges we were passing. It started quite casually, when she noticed I was reading a book about architecture and asked whether I was a student. From there we ended up talking for nearly two hours, until the lights in the carriage were dimmed. She described what it was like to work on huge projects at a time when most of the calculations were still done by hand, and she had some fascinating stories about things going wrong and how her team had fixed them. What made it so interesting was that she talked about her work with real passion, even decades later, and she was genuinely curious about my plans as well, rather than just lecturing me. It made me realise how much you can learn from people you would normally never meet, if you're willing to start a conversation.

part2.modelAnswer: If I could change one thing about my neighbourhood, I'd turn the main street into a mostly pedestrian area with proper cycle lanes. At the moment it's a narrow road lined with shops, but it's always jammed with cars and delivery vans, and the pavements are so narrow that you sometimes have to step into the road to get past people. I think it could be done gradually. The council could start by banning private cars during the busiest hours, while still allowing deliveries early in the morning, and then widen the pavements and plant a few trees. A lot of different people would benefit. Shop owners would probably see more customers, because people tend to linger when they're not dodging traffic, and parents with pushchairs and elderly residents would feel much safer. I also think the air quality would improve noticeably. The main reason I think it's necessary is that the street is the heart of the area, yet at the moment it feels like somewhere you hurry through rather than somewhere you'd want to spend time.

part2.cue: Describe a time when you learned something from a mistake.

part2.modelAnswer: The mistake I'd like to talk about happened during my second year at university, when I was responsible for booking a venue for a student society event. I was quite disorganised at the time, and I confirmed the booking by phone without asking for anything in writing. On the day itself, about sixty people turned up, only to find that the hall had been given to another group. It was incredibly embarrassing, and we ended up holding the event in a cramped classroom, which wasn't really suitable. Afterwards I felt terrible, because a lot of people had put work into the evening and I'd let them down. However, the experience taught me a valuable lesson about checking details and keeping records. Since then I've always asked for written confirmation of anything important, and I keep a simple checklist for every event or trip I organise. I'd say I also learned how to take responsibility. Rather than making excuses, I apologised to the committee and offered to sort out a refund for the snacks, and I think people respected that.

part2.modelAnswer: The piece I'd like to talk about is a slow instrumental song that my grandfather used to play on an old guitar when I was little. I'm not even sure it has a proper title, because he learned it by ear from a neighbour when he was young. I first heard it when I was about five, during summer holidays at my grandparents' house, where he would play in the evenings while we sat outside. After he passed away, I couldn't find it anywhere, but a few years ago my uncle found an old cassette recording, and I had it converted into a digital file. Now I listen to it maybe once or twice a month, usually late at night or when I'm feeling homesick. It's important to me because it brings back very vivid memories of those evenings, the smell of the garden and the sound of insects in the background. More than that, it reminds me of my grandfather's patience and gentleness, and I like the idea that a small, unrecorded piece of family history has been preserved.

part2.modelAnswer: One occasion that comes to mind is when I had to entertain my young nephew for a whole rainy weekend while his parents were away. There was no internet connection at the house we were staying in, and he'd already got bored of the few toys he'd brought, so I really had to think on my feet. In the end, I decided to turn the house into a kind of adventure story. I hid clues in different rooms, drew a treasure map on the back of an old calendar and invented a character, a pirate who'd supposedly lost his golden spoon. Each clue led to a small challenge, like building a bridge out of books or remembering a sequence of sounds. By the Sunday he was adding his own ideas to the story, which was the best part. I felt surprisingly proud of the result, partly because it was such a simple idea and cost nothing, but mainly because I saw how much he enjoyed being part of the story rather than just watching a screen. It made me realise that I'm more creative than I usually give myself credit for.

part2.modelAnswer: The person I'd like to talk about is a family friend who works as a sound designer for theatre productions. I've known her since I was a child, because she lived in the flat below ours, and over the years she's told me a lot about her work, and she's even taken me backstage a couple of times. Basically, her job is to create every sound the audience hears apart from the actors' voices, so that includes music, background noises like rain or traffic, and special effects such as a door slamming offstage. What surprised me is how much of it she records herself. She once spent a whole afternoon recording different kinds of footsteps in gravel for a single scene. I think the job is fascinating because it combines technical skill with creativity, and because when it's done well, audiences don't even notice it. It just makes the story feel real. I also admire the fact that she has to work under a lot of pressure, as everything has to be perfectly timed during live performances, with no second chances.

When they arrived, I was disappointed almost straight away. They looked much cheaper than in the photos, the battery barely lasted three hours instead of the twenty that were promised, and the left earpiece kept disconnecting. At first I tried resetting them and updating the software, but nothing worked. I contacted the seller and, to their credit, they offered a refund, but only if I paid to send them back abroad, which would have cost almost half the original price. In the end I decided to do it anyway, partly on principle. I also left an honest review explaining the problems, because I felt other buyers deserved to know. The experience taught me to be much more sceptical of online adverts and to check where a seller is actually based before I order anything.

part2.modelAnswer: The view I'd like to describe is one I saw from the top of a hill near the coast, during a walking trip with two friends last autumn. We'd set off before dawn because we wanted to reach the summit in time for sunrise, and for most of the climb it was so dark that we were walking by torchlight. When we finally got to the top, the sky was just starting to change colour. Below us there was a long, curved bay, with a small fishing village at one end, and the sea was completely still, almost like a mirror. As the sun came up, the light gradually spread across the water and the fog in the valleys behind us turned a sort of pale gold. None of us said anything for a few minutes. I think what made it so beautiful wasn't just the scenery itself but the contrast with the effort it took to get there. After hours of climbing in the cold and dark, the sudden calm and space felt almost unreal, and it's a moment I still think about when life gets hectic.

part2.modelAnswer: I'd like to talk about a group project I did in my final year at university, where four of us had to design a small survey and present our findings to a panel of lecturers. I ended up taking on the role of coordinator, partly because nobody else wanted to, and partly because I'm quite good at keeping track of deadlines. I set up a shared calendar, split the work according to people's strengths and arranged short weekly check-ins. There were a few tense moments, especially when one section was handed in late, but we talked it through rather than letting it turn into an argument. Overall, I felt it was a really rewarding experience. We got a good mark, but more importantly I learned that a team works best when people's differences are treated as an advantage rather than a problem.
part2.band6: I want to talk about a group project in my university. We were four students and we must make a survey and then present the result to the teachers. The people in my team were very different. One girl was very organised, one boy was good at statistics but he is shy, and another boy was lazy and always late. I was the leader because nobody want to do it and I am good with deadlines. I made a calendar online and I gave everyone a part of the work. We got a good mark and I learned that different people can work together well if everyone do their part.

part2.modelAnswer: The habit I'd really like to change is checking my phone the moment I wake up. The main reason I want to stop is that it puts me in a reactive frame of mind for the whole day. If I see a stressful email or a piece of bad news first thing, it tends to colour my mood, and I've noticed I'm less focused on the things I'd actually planned to do. It also makes me late more often than I'd like to admit. My plan is fairly simple. Now every morning I check my messages, news and social media in the bed, and sometimes it is twenty minutes. I want to change because it makes me stressed. If I read a bad email or bad news in the morning, I feel bad all day, and I cannot focus on my work. Also I am late sometimes because of this. part2.modelAnswer: The building I find most attractive in my city is the central library, which stands on a corner of the main square, opposite the town hall. It was built about ten years ago, and at first a lot of people criticised it because it looked so different from the older buildings around it. From the outside it's a tall, glass-fronted building with a roof that slopes down towards the square, and the lower floors are partly covered in wooden panels, which soften the overall effect. Inside there's a huge open atrium with stairs that wind up through the middle, and every floor has wide windows looking out over the city. Apart from books, it's used for exhibitions, language classes and community events, and there's a café on the ground floor that's always busy. Outside there is a lot of glass and also some wood, and the roof goes down to the square. Inside there is a big open space and stairs in the middle, and you can see the city from the windows. People go there for borrowing books, but also for exhibitions and classes, and there is a café which is always full. I think it is beautiful because it is modern but it is not cold, the wood and the light make it warm. And from the street you can see people studying, I like that.

part2.cue: Describe a time when you taught someone something.

part2.modelAnswer: I'd like to talk about the time I taught my grandmother how to make video calls on a tablet. It was during a period when the family couldn't visit her for several months, and she was feeling quite isolated, so my parents bought her a tablet and asked me to help her use it. At first it was harder than I expected. She'd never used a touchscreen before, and things that seem obvious to me, like swiping or knowing which icon to press, were completely new to her. So I slowed right down. I wrote simple step-by-step instructions on a card in large handwriting, with little drawings of each icon, and we practised the same call over and over again, first with me sitting next to her and then with me calling from the next room. After about a week she could do it on her own, and soon she was calling relatives I hardly ever speak to myself. I felt really proud, but also a bit humbled, because it showed me how much patience good teaching requires, and how easy it is to forget what it's like to be a complete beginner.
part2.band6: I will talk about when I taught my grandmother to do video calls. At that time we could not visit her for some months and she was lonely, so my parents bought her a tablet and I helped her. It was more difficult than I think. She never used a touchscreen before, so she did not know how to swipe or which button she has to press. So I went very slowly. I wrote the steps on a card with big letters and small pictures, and we practised many times. First I was next to her and then I called her from another room. After one week she can do it alone, and then she started to call all the family. I felt very proud of her. Also I understood that teaching needs a lot of patience, it is not easy.

notes.fc: Band 6 is coherent but the ending is short and general ('it is not easy'). Band 7 reflects on the experience with a two-part conclusion, showing the speaker can keep going and develop ideas.
notes.lr: Band 7: 'isolated', 'slowed right down', 'over and over again', 'humbled', 'a complete beginner'. Band 6 uses 'lonely' and 'button' acceptably but with less range.
notes.gra: Band 6: 'more difficult than I think', 'She never used' (needs past perfect), 'she has to press', 'she can do it alone'. Band 7 uses past perfect, comparison and 'how much patience good teaching requires' accurately.
notes.pron: The band 7 answer has long sentences; practise breathing at commas and keeping a steady rhythm. Stress 'slowed RIGHT DOWN' and 'over and OVER again' for natural emphasis.

part2.cue: Describe a time when you were surprised by something.
bullets: and explain why it surprised you
part3: Do people generally like surprises, or do they prefer to know what will happen?
Is it a good idea to organise surprise parties?
Why do some news stories surprise people more than others?
How can unexpected events help people grow?

part2.modelAnswer: One thing that genuinely surprised me happened last winter, when I went to a small jazz concert with a colleague. It was in a basement venue in the city centre, and to be honest I only went because she had a spare ticket. Halfway through the evening, the bandleader announced that a guest would be joining them, and to my astonishment it was my old maths teacher from secondary school, who walked on stage carrying a saxophone. I'd had no idea that he played any instrument at all. At school he'd always come across as rather strict and serious, and I'd never imagined him having a life outside the classroom, let alone performing in front of an audience. And he was brilliant. He played several solos and was clearly enjoying himself enormously. During the break I went up to say hello, and he laughed and admitted that very few of his students knew. I think it surprised me so much because it completely changed my picture of him, and it reminded me that we often judge people by the single role we see them in.
part2.band6: I want to talk about a surprise last winter. My colleague had one more ticket for a jazz concert so I went with her. The concert was in a small place under the ground in the city centre. In the middle of the concert the leader of the band said there is a special guest, and it was my maths teacher from high school! He came with a saxophone. I never knew that he can play music. In school he was very strict and serious, so I could not imagine that he has a hobby like this. He played really well and he looked very happy. In the break I said hello to him and he laughed and said not many students know about it. It surprised me because I had a different idea about him, and now I know that people can be very different outside their job.

notes.fc: Both answers tell the story in order. Band 7 builds suspense ('Halfway through the evening', 'to my astonishment') and closes with a general insight; band 6 reaches the same point but in plainer steps.
notes.lr: Band 7: 'basement venue', 'come across as', 'let alone', 'judge people by the single role'. Band 6 says 'a small place under the ground', which shows a vocabulary gap being worked around.
notes.gra: Band 6 errors in reported speech and sequence: 'said there is', 'I never knew that he can play', 'not many students know'. Band 7 backshifts correctly and uses past perfect ('I'd had no idea', 'he'd always come across').
notes.pron: Use a higher pitch and pause before the surprise ('and to my astonishment... it was my old maths teacher'). Band 6 speakers often deliver the key moment at the same pitch as everything else.

part2.modelAnswer: A series I really enjoy is a nature documentary series that follows a team of wildlife researchers working in remote parts of the world. Each episode focuses on a single animal or habitat, for instance snow leopards in the mountains or the coral reefs of a particular island. I came across it more or less by accident, when the streaming service I use recommended it after I'd watched a programme about volcanoes. I usually watch an episode on Sunday evenings, when I've finished everything for the week and want something calm but still interesting. What I like most about it is that it doesn't just show beautiful scenery. It also shows the scientists' day-to-day work, including the frustrating parts, like waiting for weeks in a hide without seeing anything. That makes it feel honest rather than staged. I've also learned a surprising amount from it, for example about how climate change is affecting migration patterns. And the photography is stunning, so it's a good reminder of how much of the natural world I've never seen and probably never will.

part2.modelAnswer: I'd like to describe a decision I had to make at an airport about three years ago. I was on my way to a friend's wedding, and my first flight was delayed so badly that I was certain to miss my connection. When I got to the airline desk, the agent told me I had two options: wait nine hours for the next direct flight, which would get me there after the ceremony, or take a flight leaving in twenty minutes to a different city and then catch an overnight bus. There was a queue of angry passengers behind me, so I had about thirty seconds to choose. I went for the second option, ran to the gate and only just made it. The bus journey was long and uncomfortable, and I arrived exhausted and slightly crumpled, but I was there in time to see my friend get married. Afterwards, I felt very relieved and quite proud of myself, because I'm normally someone who likes to weigh everything up carefully. It showed me that sometimes a decision that's good enough, made quickly, is better than a perfect one made too late.

part2.modelAnswer: A period I'd like to know much more about is the early days of long-distance sea trade in Asia, roughly between the ninth and fifteenth centuries. What I know at the moment is fairly basic. I'm aware that merchants travelled huge distances by ship, carrying goods such as ceramics, spices and textiles, and that ports along the coast grew into wealthy, multicultural cities as a result. I also know that archaeologists have found shipwrecks with thousands of pieces of pottery still intact. I'd like to learn more in a few different ways. I'd love to visit a maritime museum where some of these wrecks are displayed, and I'd probably start by reading a well-written general history to get the bigger picture before going into detail. I'm interested in it mainly because it shows how connected the world was long before modern technology. People from very different cultures were trading, exchanging ideas and even intermarrying, and I find that a useful reminder that globalisation isn't really a new phenomenon, even though we often talk about it as if it were.

part2.modelAnswer: The person I'd like to talk about is the pharmacist who runs a small pharmacy near my parents' home. Her name is Linh, and I've known her for more than ten years, because my family has always gone to her shop, and I even did a short work-experience placement there when I was at school. Obviously her job involves preparing prescriptions and selling medicines, but in practice she does much more than that. A lot of older people in the area go to her for advice before they'd ever consider booking an appointment with a doctor. I think she's exceptionally good at her job for a few reasons. Firstly, she's extremely careful. I've seen her phone a doctor to double-check a dose when something didn't look right. Secondly, she explains things clearly, without using jargon, and she always makes sure people understand when and how to take their medication. But what really stands out is how she remembers her customers. She'll ask an elderly man how his knee is or whether a child's cough has cleared up, so people feel that she genuinely cares about them.

part2.modelAnswer: The activity I'd like to talk about is kayaking, which I tried for the first time last summer. A friend of mine had been doing it for years, and she kept telling me that I'd love it, so eventually I agreed to join her on a beginner's trip along a quiet river about an hour outside the city. There were six of us in the group, plus an instructor who spent the first half hour teaching us how to hold the paddle properly and, more importantly, what to do if the kayak tipped over. I have to admit that I was quite nervous at the start, because I'm not a particularly strong swimmer. For the first twenty minutes I kept going round in circles, which was a bit embarrassing, but once I got the hang of it I started to really enjoy it. The river was surrounded by forest, and it was so quiet that we could hear birds and the sound of the paddles in the water. I felt a real sense of achievement by the end of the day, and I've since been back three more times.

part2.modelAnswer: A rule I think is really important is one we had at my last workplace, which was a small design company. The rule was that nobody was allowed to send a document to a client without a second person checking it first. It applied to everything, from short emails with attached quotes to final designs. If someone broke the rule, there wasn't a formal punishment as such, but the manager would sit down with them and go through what could have gone wrong, and if it happened again it would be mentioned in their annual review. At first some people found it annoying, because it slowed things down, especially when deadlines were tight. However, I think it's important for several reasons. Most obviously, it caught a lot of mistakes, such as wrong prices or spelling errors in a client's name, which could have been really embarrassing. But it also meant that responsibility was shared, so nobody felt they had to be perfect on their own. And I think it encouraged people to learn from each other, because you often picked up useful ideas by checking someone else's work.

It's about five hours from my city by bus, followed by a short drive up a winding road, so I don't get the chance to go very often. Her house is an old wooden building with a big vegetable garden at the back and a view across the valley. We didn't do anything particularly exciting, but that was part of the charm. In the mornings I helped her in the garden, picking herbs and planting beans, and in the afternoons we went for long walks or visited her neighbours, who all seemed to know who I was before I'd even introduced myself. In the evenings we cooked together and talked for hours about family stories I'd never heard before. I felt incredibly relaxed by the end of it. Living in a busy city, I'd almost forgotten what it was like to have no schedule at all, and the visit made me realise I should make more of an effort to see her.

I also cut back on things like eating out and buying new clothes, which was harder than I expected, because my friends were going out a lot that year. When I finally went to the shop and bought it, I felt a huge sense of satisfaction, partly because it was the most expensive thing I'd ever bought with my own money. It was held in the main lecture theatre, which was packed because it was open to the public as well as to students. The talk was about what she called 'urban heat islands', which are areas of a city that become much hotter than the surrounding countryside because of concrete, asphalt and a lack of trees. She showed thermal images of the same street before and after trees had been planted, and the difference in surface temperature was quite dramatic. I found it interesting for a couple of reasons. Firstly, she explained a fairly technical subject in a way that anyone could follow, using everyday examples like why a car parked in the sun becomes so hot. Secondly, it was very practical. She talked about cheap solutions, such as painting roofs white and creating small green spaces, which made the problem feel solvable rather than hopeless. I've noticed shade and trees in my city much more since then.

As for how long it would take, I imagine I could make something simple, like a small shelf, within a couple of months, but to become genuinely skilled would probably take several years of regular practice. part2.modelAnswer: The skill I'd like to talk about is bread-making, which my grandmother taught me when I was about eleven. She had made bread every Sunday for as long as I could remember, and one afternoon she simply handed me the flour and told me to start. My first loaves were flat and far too dense, and she was very patient about it. We practised together most weekends for almost a year. She would show me how to tell when the dough had been kneaded enough, by pressing it with a finger and watching whether it sprang back. What I value most is that the lessons were never really about bread. She taught me to be patient with a task that goes wrong and to try again without getting upset. Today I still bake for my own family, and every time the kitchen smells of fresh bread, I'm reminded of her. The skill is useful in a practical way, because I save money and eat better, but its real value is the habit of patience she gave me.
part2.band6: I want to talk about a skill my grandmother taught me, it is making bread. I was about eleven years old when I started learning. At first my bread was not good, it was very hard and flat. But my grandmother was very patient and she showed me many times. We practised together every weekend for one year. She told me how to check the dough, you press it with your finger and if it goes back up then it is ready. This skill is useful for me now because I can make bread for my family and I do not need to buy it from the shop. It also helps me to relax after a long day at work. My grandmother is not alive now, but when I bake I remember her and I am very grateful for her lessons. I think this is a very good skill to learn from family.

notes.fc: Band 6 tells the story in a flat sequence and ends with a general opinion. Band 7 gives the turning point (the first failed loaves), explains the lesson beyond the skill itself, and closes with a reason that adds something new.
notes.lr: Band 6 repeats 'very' and 'good' and uses 'the skill' loosely. Band 7 uses precise items such as 'kneaded enough', 'sprang back' and 'went wrong', and paraphrases its own points.
notes.gra: Band 6 has tense slips in the narrative and a comma splice ('it is making bread'). Band 7 mixes past simple and past perfect ('had made', 'had been kneaded') and uses a relative clause to add information.
notes.pron: Stress the content words in 'the lessons were never really about bread', and pause after 'patient' to let the contrast land. Band 6 speakers often give every word equal stress, which hides the point.
